newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus, Turkey dismiss US claim that crisis over.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus, Turkey dismiss US claim that crisis over.

text.p: Cyprus dismissed talk of a deal to ease tension and Turkey said on Tuesday nothing had change, dismissing a U.S. claim that a looming crisis between the two countries was over.

U.S. envoy Carey Cavanaugh left Cyprus on Monday talking of an imminent breakthrough to ease tension along the ceasefire line separating Greek and Turkish Cypriots on the Mediterranean island. In Athens, he said on Tuesday the crisis about Cypriot plans to deploy missiles was over.

But Cyprus called the U.S. comments on the ceasefire line a misunderstanding and Turkey followed with fresh warnings to Greece and the Cypriot government that the crisis over the plan to buy Russian-made anti-aircraft missiles was not over.
Cyprus says the missiles are for self-defence, but Turkey calls them a threat.

Despite the reaction of Cyprus and Turkey, some observers thought Cavanaugh had eased tension by announcing after seeing Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides on Monday that the missiles would not be installed for 16 months.

"He reduced tension just by saying it was reduced," one Western diplomat in capital Nicosia said. "The fact that the Americans have said the situation is defusing is enough. It may not show now but that view will soon make it to Turkey."
But Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan renewed his calls for Cyprus to end plans to deploy the missiles, which have a range of 150 km (90 miles) and could reach Turkey.
"It is wrong to turn Cyprus into a barrel of gunpowder. I hope Greece and Greek Cyprus give up these intolerable provocations and get smart," Erbakan said.

Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash said in north Cyprus that the crisis remained: "Of course it's continuing...Clerides has neither made a sacrifice nor a gesture. So what is going to happen after 16 months?"

The Cypriot government said the 16 month-period before deploying the missiles is enough to find a solution to the 23-year-old division of the island -- but it will deploy the missiles if there is no solution.
It has shrugged off Western criticism and Turkish threats, saying it needs missiles to protect Greek Cypriot areas of the island from Turkey, which occupies its northern third.
The Cypriot government dismissed Cavanaugh's assertion the two sides were close to a military agreement on ways to reduce tension along the ceasefire line.

Yiannakis Cassoulides, Cypriot government spokesman, said: "President Clerides has reiterated to Mr Cavanaugh his intention to intervene in the military dialogue with our own military people and see what is happening with the dialogue and try to help it to advance. That's all."
The U.N. proposals relate to unloading weapons along the 180-km (110-mile) ceasefire line and abandonning sentry posts. They also impose a code of conduct on soldiers.
Four Greek Cypriots and one Turkish Cypriot soldier have been killed in incidents along the U.N.-patrolled buffer zone since June, raising tension.

Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when Turkey invaded the north of the island after a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece. Turkey has about 30,000 troops in the north while the internationally recognised Cypriot government has 11,500 in the south.
